rationale: The sole existing example, verified by 62/329, applies a red-hot ring to a person's body. Clarifies the physical branding component beyond an ordinary ink-stamping interpretation; no separate sense or new semantic attestation.

summary: 62/329 explicitly heats the ring red-hot and presses it against the husband's body before dməġla. This supports the gloss clarification 'ein Brandzeichen einbrennen'.
The verb has a feminine l-series agent suffix; the affected person and instrument are recoverable from the coordinated preceding clauses, not separately marked arguments of this final verb.
The inherited Turkish damga etymology is retained. This is a directly inflected loan-derived verb, not an attested light verb plus noun construction.
One occurrence already quoted supplies the whole evidence base; no new form, additional example or productivity claim.
Does dmġ also apply to ink stamps, seals or other marking, or primarily branding? The present evidence establishes only bodily hot branding.
Is the affected person normally an overt object or suffix when the verb stands without the preceding action sequence?
